intro:
These exercises take packaging from an afterthought at the end of a build script to a first-class operations contract. The chapter's central claim is that one crate graph can legitimately ship in several shapes — a static Linux binary, a container image, a browser Wasm module, a native library for a foreign host — and that each shape carries different runtime assumptions, different feature gates, and different validation. The work here is to make those differences explicit data instead of tribal knowledge buried in release scripts.

The exercises move from describing the artifact matrix, to reading a multi-stage Docker build, to implementing target-aware artifact naming, to designing the feature policy, supply-chain gates, and rollback story that turn a successful compile into an operable release. The throughline is the chapter's most expensive bug: not a compiler failure, but a green release whose final artifact was never tested in the runtime shape production actually executes.

exerciseSolutions.title: Create a packaging matrix for native, container, wasm, and library outputs
exerciseSolutions.solution:
A packaging matrix is useful only when every row answers two questions: who runs this artifact, and what does it assume about its runtime. Collapsing all four outputs into one vague "build" hides exactly the differences that cause production incidents, so the first job is to give each consumer its own row with a distinct target triple or crate type.

The four rows differ on crate type and target before they differ on anything else. The fleet binary is a `bin` crate built for `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`; choosing musl over gnu is a deliberate decision to statically link libc so the binary does not depend on the host's glibc version. The container is the same `bin` crate, but the artifact is an image tag in a registry, and its runtime assumption is the base image, not the host. The browser bundle is built `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and is consumed through JavaScript glue (the loader and bindings), so its runtime is the browser's Wasm engine, not libc at all. The native library is a `cdylib` (or `staticlib`) crate built for the foreign host's triple, and its runtime assumption is a stable C ABI that the C++ host links against.

Feature gates should differ per row precisely because consumers differ. The fleet binary and container can share most features, but the Wasm bundle must drop anything that touches the filesystem, threads it cannot spawn, or native TLS — it carries a browser-shaped feature set. The native library should expose only the FFI surface the host needs, with server-only features gated off, because every extra symbol is attack surface in someone else's process.

Validation has to be per row because the failure modes are per row. The native binary deserves a smoke run on a musl-like environment, not just on the build host. The container deserves a boot-and-health-check against the actual image. The Wasm bundle deserves an instantiation test in a headless browser or Node Wasm runtime to confirm the glue loads. The native library deserves a tiny C/C++ harness that links it and calls one exported function, because "it compiled" says nothing about whether the ABI contract holds.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The matrix encoded as data so each row's target, runtime assumption, and smoke test are explicit rather than implicit.
criteria: Four rows each carry a distinct target triple or crate type (musl bin, gnu image, wasm cdylib, host-triple cdylib).
Each row names a runtime assumption: static libc, base image plus CA certs, browser engine plus glue, foreign C ABI.
Each row carries an artifact-specific smoke test, from a musl sandbox run to a C harness linking the native library.

exerciseSolutions.title: Review a Docker multi-stage build and its minimal runtime image
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The builder stage owns the entire toolchain: the Rust compiler, Cargo, the dependency cache, source, build scripts, and intermediate object files. None of that should leak into the runtime stage. A multi-stage build exists precisely so the runtime image inherits only the finished executable and nothing that could be used to recompile, inspect, or pivot. If the toolchain bleeds through, the image is both larger and a richer target.

The runtime stage needs more than the executable, and this is where a `scratch` image bites. A `scratch` image is genuinely empty: no CA certificate bundle, no `/etc/passwd`, no timezone data, no `/tmp`. A service that makes outbound TLS calls will fail certificate verification because there are no root CAs to trust — so the build must copy `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` in explicitly. If the process should not run as root, the runtime stage must create a non-root user and set `USER`, but `scratch` has no `adduser`, so the uid/gid and a minimal passwd entry have to be staged from the builder. Any code that resolves timezones, reads `/etc/resolv.conf`, or writes a temp file also assumes files that `scratch` does not provide. And the musl-versus-gnu linkage matters here: a glibc-linked binary copied into `scratch` will not find the dynamic loader and will fail to start; either link statically with musl or copy the loader and shared objects.

Distroless or Alpine is calmer than `scratch` when the workload needs a real, if minimal, userland. Distroless ships CA certificates, a non-root user, and tzdata while still excluding a shell and package manager, which keeps the attack surface small without the missing-file surprises. Alpine adds a shell and apk, which is handy for debugging and for binaries that genuinely need a libc present, at the cost of a slightly larger surface. The rule of thumb: reach for `scratch` only for a fully static binary with no filesystem expectations; otherwise distroless is the saner default.

The final smoke test must run against the image, not against the binary on the build host. The build host has CA certs, a passwd file, and a full libc that the image may lack, so a binary that runs there proves nothing about the image. The image-level test boots the container and exercises a real path: hit `/healthz`, make one outbound TLS request, and confirm the process is running as the expected non-root user. That is the only test that catches the missing-CA-bundle and missing-loader failures before operators do.
exerciseSolutions.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---- builder stage: owns the toolchain, source, and caches ----
FROM rust:1.79 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY Cargo.toml Cargo.lock ./
COPY src ./src
# Static musl link so the artifact has no glibc/loader dependency.
RUN rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl \
 && cargo build --release --locked --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl

# ---- runtime stage: scratch needs files that scratch does not ship ----
FROM scratch AS runtime
# CA bundle, or outbound TLS fails with no roots to trust.
COPY --from=builder /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/
# A passwd entry so we can run as a real non-root uid instead of root.
COPY --from=builder /etc/passwd /etc/passwd
COPY --from=builder \
  /src/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/gateway /usr/local/bin/gateway
USER 10001:10001
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/gateway"]

# Image-level smoke test (run in CI against the built image, not the host binary):
#   docker run -d --name smoke -p 8080:8080 gateway:ci
#   docker exec smoke /usr/local/bin/gateway --version   # process actually starts
#   curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/healthz              # health path responds
#   # and one outbound TLS call to prove the CA bundle is present and trusted
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A scratch runtime stage that explicitly stages the CA bundle, passwd entry, and a non-root user, with an image-level smoke test rather than a host-binary check.
criteria: Builder and runtime responsibilities are separated: the toolchain and caches stay in the builder, only the executable plus needed files reach runtime.
Names concrete missing runtime dependencies a scratch image lacks: CA certificate bundle, passwd entry, non-root user, dynamic loader for glibc binaries.
Justifies distroless/Alpine over scratch with a workload reason — userland files and debuggability versus a fully static binary with no filesystem needs.

exerciseSolutions.title: Implement a packaging matrix for native, container, and wasm builds
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The point of this exercise is release contracts, not formatting. Each target class has a different naming convention because each has a different consumer, so the implementation routes a single `Target` value to exactly one naming rule via a `match`. The compiler then forces every variant to be handled, which is the property you want: adding a fourth target forces a decision rather than silently falling through to a default.

The native output carries the full target triple as a suffix — `pricing-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`. Encoding the triple in the filename means two fleet hosts can never disagree about which linkage they received, and an operator can read the libc decision straight off the artifact name. The container output is shaped like a registry tag — `ghcr.io/acme/pricing:1.2.0` — because its consumer is an orchestrator pulling from a registry, and the version belongs in the tag, not in a file suffix. The Wasm output is named like a Wasm artifact — `pricing-wasm32-unknown-unknown.wasm` — never like a native binary, because its consumer is a browser loader that expects a `.wasm` module, and the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` segment records that this is the browser target rather than WASI.

The enum keeps the target set closed and explicit. There is no string-typed `target: &str` that could receive a typo or an unsupported value; the only inputs are the three variants, and `match` is exhaustive over them. This is the same move the chapter makes with `BuildTarget` and `is_static`: encode intent as data the compiler can check, not as a convention hidden in a script.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One Target value routes through an exhaustive match to exactly one naming convention per consumer; this is the lab solution.
criteria: The enum has three distinct variants — Native, Container, Wasm — keeping the target set closed and exhaustively matched.
The function returns three different naming shapes: a triple-suffixed filename, a registry tag, and a .wasm artifact name.
The program prints the expected native, container, and wasm names exactly (verified by compiling and running).

exerciseSolutions.title: Design a feature-gated release workflow
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is a catch-all default feature set: `metrics`, `admin`, optional native bindings, and `browser` all ship by default even though most service deployments need only the core server. The cost is concrete — every default feature pulls dependencies, enlarges the binary, and widens attack surface for deployments that never use it. The fix is to make the default set the smallest honest server and move everything else opt-in, so the common deployment builds the smallest correct artifact and an expanded build is a deliberate choice.

Concretely: `default = ["server"]` and nothing more. `metrics` becomes opt-in because a deployment without a metrics sink does not need the exporter dependency or the endpoint. `admin` becomes opt-in and, importantly, gating it off removes a whole privileged surface from production images that do not run the admin host. The native bindings move behind `native` because they only matter when a foreign host embeds the library, and `browser` moves behind its own feature because it pulls Wasm-shaped dependencies that have no place in a server build. None of these belong in `default`.

The distinction the exercise is really probing: not every optional behavior belongs behind a compile-time flag. A feature gate is the right tool when the choice changes which code and dependencies are compiled in — `metrics` pulling an exporter, `admin` adding endpoints and their auth surface, `native`/`browser` changing the crate type and target. A runtime setting is the right tool when the same binary should behave differently per environment: the metrics scrape interval, the admin bind address, log level, sampling rate, feature flags for product behavior. Compiling the same binary three times to change a port number is a packaging smell; that belongs in config, environment, or a flag, read at startup.

CI must build at least three combinations so the smallest honest artifact is provably buildable and testable: `--no-default-features` plus `--features minimal` (or just `server`) for the lean lane, `default` for the common case, and `--features server,metrics,admin` (or `--all-features`) for the expanded lane. Building only `default` lets a `minimal` build rot until release day. The signal to compare before and after is twofold: artifact size (stripped binary bytes and image size) and attack surface (dependency count from `cargo tree`, and the set of exposed endpoints and exported symbols). A leaner default should show fewer transitive crates and a smaller binary, which is the measurable payoff of moving features out of `default`.
exerciseSolutions.code:
# Cargo.toml — default is the smallest honest server; everything else opt-in.
[features]
default = ["server"]

# Core: the server that every service deployment actually runs.
server  = ["dep:axum", "dep:tokio"]

# Opt-in: each changes which code/deps compile in, so each is a real
# packaging decision rather than a runtime knob.
minimal = []                       # explicit lean alias for the smallest build
metrics = ["dep:metrics-exporter"] # adds an exporter dependency + endpoint
admin   = ["server", "dep:admin-auth"] # adds a privileged surface
native  = ["dep:cbindgen-runtime"] # only when a foreign host embeds the lib
browser = ["dep:wasm-bindgen"]     # wasm-shaped deps, no place in a server build

# CI feature matrix (e.g. in a GitHub Actions strategy):
#   lane: minimal   -> cargo test --no-default-features --features minimal
#   lane: default   -> cargo test
#   lane: expanded  -> cargo test --features server,metrics,admin
#
# Compare before/after:
#   cargo tree --no-default-features --features minimal | wc -l   # dep count
#   cargo tree --all-features | wc -l
#   ls -l target/release/gateway                                  # stripped bytes
#
# Runtime settings that must NOT become features (same binary, different env):
#   - metrics scrape interval, admin bind address, log level, sample rate
#   These are read from config/env at startup, not selected at compile time.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A feature policy with a minimal default plus opt-in features, an explicit CI matrix, and the runtime-versus-compile-time boundary.
criteria: Moves non-core features (metrics, admin, native, browser) out of default, leaving default as the smallest honest server.
Defines at least two explicit CI feature combinations — minimal, default, and an expanded server+metrics+admin lane.
Distinguishes runtime config (scrape interval, bind address, log level) from compile-time packaging features, and compares dep count and binary size before/after.

exerciseSolutions.title: Add supply-chain checks to CI before release day forces the issue
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The current pipeline tests and publishes but produces no trust data: no checksums, no SBOM, no dependency-policy or advisory gate. The fix is to split the release lane into checks that run before publication (gates that can stop a release) and metadata that is generated after the artifact is built (so it describes the exact bytes operators will download). Mixing these up — for example, generating an SBOM from source rather than from the built artifact, or running advisory checks after publish — produces metadata that does not match what shipped and gates that cannot prevent a bad release.

Before publication, run the gates. `cargo audit` (RustSec advisory database) checks for known vulnerabilities in the dependency tree and should be a hard gate: a known-exploitable transitive dependency stops the release. `cargo deny check` enforces dependency policy — license allowlists, banned crates, duplicate versions, and untrusted sources — and is also a gate, because policy violations are decisions the team has already made. These run against the locked dependency graph before any artifact is published.

After the artifact is built, generate the metadata that travels with it: a checksum (SHA-256) of each final artifact, a cryptographic signature over those artifacts (or over the checksum manifest), an SBOM generated from the built artifact (for example with `cargo cyclonedx` or `syft` against the binary/image), and build provenance attestation that records how and from what commit the artifact was produced. The chapter's rule applies directly: generated metadata is only useful if it follows the final artifact users actually download, so the SBOM and checksums must be computed from the published binary and image, not from a separate source-only pass.

The gate-versus-advisory split is a judgment call the team should make explicitly. Treat known-vulnerability advisories and license/policy violations as hard gates — they block. Treat informational signals as advisory: unmaintained-crate warnings, yanked-but-not-vulnerable versions, or new-but-unreviewed transitive additions can warn without blocking, so the pipeline is not so brittle that every upstream advisory halts shipping. Whatever the split, it must be written down in `deny.toml` and the audit config rather than living in someone's head.

Finally, the pipeline must fail unambiguously. Each gate runs as its own named step with a non-zero exit on failure, so the CI UI shows exactly which gate blocked publication ("cargo-audit: RUSTSEC-2024-xxxx in openssl") rather than a generic red X. Publication is a separate job that depends on every gate passing, so a blocked release never leaves artifacts half-published — the release state is either fully gated-and-signed or not published at all.
exerciseSolutions.code:
# release.yml — gates before publish, trust metadata after build.

jobs:
  # ---- gates: any failure stops the release with a named reason ----
  audit:
    steps:
      - run: cargo audit --deny warnings        # RustSec advisories = hard gate
  policy:
    steps:
      - run: cargo deny check licenses bans sources advisories  # policy gate

  build:
    needs: [audit, policy]
    steps:
      - run: cargo build --release --locked --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl

  # ---- metadata: generated from the BUILT artifact, travels with it ----
  attest:
    needs: [build]
    steps:
      # checksum the exact bytes operators will download
      - run: sha256sum target/.../release/gateway > gateway.sha256
      # SBOM from the built artifact, not a source-only pass
      - run: syft target/.../release/gateway -o cyclonedx-json > gateway.sbom.json
      # signature over the checksum manifest
      - run: cosign sign-blob --yes gateway.sha256 > gateway.sig
      # build provenance: commit, builder, inputs
      - run: cosign attest --predicate provenance.json target/.../release/gateway

  # ---- publish only after every gate and attestation succeeds ----
  publish:
    needs: [attest]
    steps:
      # uploads binary + .sha256 + .sbom.json + .sig together so the trust
      # data follows the artifact, never lands separately.
      - run: ./scripts/publish.sh gateway gateway.sha256 gateway.sbom.json gateway.sig

# Gate vs advisory policy (written down, not tribal):
#   gate     -> known vulnerabilities, license/banned-crate violations
#   advisory -> unmaintained warnings, yanked-not-vulnerable, new transitive deps
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A release lane with audit and policy gates before build, artifact-derived checksum/SBOM/signature/provenance after build, and a publish job gated on all of them.
criteria: Defines more than three supply-chain checks/outputs: cargo audit, cargo deny, checksum, SBOM, signature, and provenance.
Places gates (audit, policy) before publication and artifact-metadata steps (checksum, SBOM, signature) after the build, all preceding publish.
Each gate is a named step with a non-zero exit, and publish depends on all gates, so a blocked release reports its reason and never leaves a half-published state.

exerciseSolutions.title: Write a release-engineering plan for a Rust service with several artifact shapes
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The repository ships three artifact classes from one source: `gateway` (the fleet binary and its container image), `gateway-wasm-admin` (a browser Wasm module for the admin dashboard), and `gateway-risk-lib` (a native library a foreign host embeds). The plan must decide what versions together, how each is validated, what gates promotion, and what rollback data is published — because operators, not the build, are the consumers of this plan.

Versioning: the binary and its container image must release together and share a version, because the image is just the binary in a runtime wrapper and splitting their versions invites the "which build is actually running" confusion the chapter warns about. `gateway-wasm-admin` can version independently when its only contract with the server is a stable wire/API surface (Chapter 19), so a dashboard fix should not force a fleet redeploy — but it pins a minimum compatible server version. `gateway-risk-lib` must version under a strict ABI contract: any change to an exported symbol's signature is a breaking version bump, because a foreign host links against the ABI, not the source.

Validation is per artifact class. The final binary gets a smoke run on a musl-like sandbox plus a `--version`/`--healthz` self-check. The final image gets a boot-and-health-check: start the container, hit `/healthz` and `/readyz`, and make one outbound TLS call to confirm the CA bundle is present. The Wasm package gets an instantiation test in a headless browser runtime that loads the module through its JS glue and calls one exported function. The native library gets a C/C++ harness that links `libgateway_risk.so` and invokes one exported symbol — the only test that proves the ABI contract holds. "It compiled" is never the smoke test; the chapter's most expensive bug is a green release whose artifact was never run in its real runtime shape.

Promotion from canary to broad rollout is gated on observability, not a timer. Hold canary at a small traffic slice and require: error rate (5xx and panic count) at or below the pre-deploy baseline, p99 latency within a defined budget, and saturation signals (memory, CPU, open file descriptors) stable — a slow memory climb under canary is the cheapest place to catch a leak. Add a health/readiness gate so the orchestrator only promotes instances reporting ready, and a business-signal check where one exists (request success on the critical path). If any signal regresses past threshold, promotion halts automatically.

Rollback data must make reverting easier than improvising, and it must point at the artifact, not the commit. Published with every release: the exact previous artifact references (the prior image digest, the prior binary checksum, the prior `gateway-risk-lib` version), the one-command rollback procedure (redeploy the prior image digest, no rebuild), the compatibility note stating which `gateway-wasm-admin` and `gateway-risk-lib` versions pair with the rolled-back server, and the database/migration direction if a schema changed. Operators roll back to a digest under pressure; they cannot rebuild from source mid-incident, so the artifact identity and the procedure must be in the release notes before anything goes wrong.
exerciseSolutions.code:
# release-plan.md — gateway, gateway-wasm-admin, gateway-risk-lib

## Versioning
# gateway (binary) + container image : release together, same version
# gateway-wasm-admin                 : independent; pins min server API version
# gateway-risk-lib                   : ABI-strict; symbol change = breaking bump

## Per-artifact smoke tests (run on the FINAL artifact, not the build host)
# binary   : run on musl sandbox; `gateway --version`; `gateway --healthz`
# image    : boot container; GET /healthz and /readyz; one outbound TLS call
# wasm     : instantiate in headless runtime via JS glue; call one export
# risk-lib : C harness links libgateway_risk.so and calls one exported symbol

## Canary -> broad promotion gates (all must hold on the canary slice)
# - 5xx rate and panic count <= pre-deploy baseline
# - p99 latency within budget
# - memory / CPU / fd saturation stable (catches leaks early)
# - orchestrator readiness: only promote instances reporting /readyz=ok
# - critical-path request success holding
# any regression past threshold => promotion halts automatically

## Rollback bundle (published WITH the release, points at artifacts not commits)
# - prior image digest:   ghcr.io/acme/gateway@sha256:<prev>
# - prior binary sha256:  <prev-checksum>
# - prior risk-lib ver:   gateway-risk-lib 4.2.1
# - procedure:            redeploy prior digest (no rebuild) -> 1 command
# - compatibility note:   wasm-admin 3.x + risk-lib 4.2.x pair with this server
# - data direction:       migration up/down notes if schema changed
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A release plan naming co-versioning, per-class smoke tests, observability promotion gates, and artifact-referenced rollback data.
criteria: Defines distinct validation for at least two artifact classes — image boot/health-check, wasm instantiation, and native-lib C harness.
Includes a promotion gate (canary observability thresholds plus readiness) and a rollback requirement (prior image digest plus a no-rebuild procedure).
Names at least two observability signals during rollout — 5xx/panic rate, p99 latency, and saturation (memory/CPU/fd).

labSolution.expectedOutput:
native = pricing-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
container = ghcr.io/acme/pricing:1.2.0
wasm = pricing-wasm32-unknown-unknown.wasm
labSolution.explanation:
The lab completes the stub `artifact_name` by replacing the placeholder that returned `app.to_string()` with an exhaustive `match` over the `Target` enum. Each arm encodes one artifact class's naming contract: `Native` builds a filename with the full `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` triple, `Container` builds a registry-qualified, version-tagged image reference `ghcr.io/acme/pricing:1.2.0`, and `Wasm` builds a `.wasm` artifact named for the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target.

Because the `match` is exhaustive over the three variants, the compiler guarantees every target has a naming rule and that adding a fourth target would force a decision rather than silently fall through. The `version` parameter is used only by the container arm, which is correct: a registry tag versions in the tag itself, whereas the native and wasm filenames identify the artifact by its target triple.

Running `main` calls `artifact_name` once per variant with `app = "pricing"` and `version = "1.2.0"`, so the three `println!` lines print the native triple-suffixed name, the registry tag, and the wasm artifact name in order — exactly the expected output. The program was compiled with `rustc --edition 2021 -O` and run; its stdout matches the expected output byte for byte.

reviewAnswers.question: What makes a static binary attractive, and what runtime assumptions can still remain outside the binary itself?
reviewAnswers.answer: A static binary (for example built for x86_64-unknown-linux-musl) is attractive because it links libc statically, so it does not depend on the host's glibc version and runs across heterogeneous fleet hosts without a matching dynamic loader. But "static" only covers code linkage, not the rest of the runtime: the binary still assumes a CA certificate bundle for outbound TLS, a /etc/passwd entry to run as a non-root user, timezone data, /etc/resolv.conf for DNS, and a writable /tmp. Those files live outside the binary, which is exactly why a static binary copied into a scratch image can compile cleanly yet fail at runtime when it tries to verify a TLS certificate with no roots present.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should browser wasm and WASI packaging be treated as different release families?
reviewAnswers.answer: They target different runtimes with different capabilities, so they are different artifacts with different validation. Browser wasm (wasm32-unknown-unknown) is consumed through JavaScript glue in a browser engine that has no filesystem, no threads it cannot spawn, and no direct syscalls, so its feature set must exclude anything that touches the OS. WASI (wasm32-wasi) targets a host that provides a standardized system interface — files, clocks, environment — so it can use capabilities the browser forbids. Treating them as one family produces a bundle that assumes the wrong runtime; each needs its own feature gates and its own smoke test (headless-browser instantiation versus a WASI runtime run).

reviewAnswers.question: When would you choose `cdylib` instead of `staticlib`, and why is the ABI contract part of release engineering?
reviewAnswers.answer: Choose cdylib when a foreign host loads the library dynamically at runtime — a shared object the host dlopens or links against and can update independently of its own rebuild — and choose staticlib when the consumer links the archive directly into its own binary at build time. Either way the exported symbols form a C ABI that the foreign host depends on, and that ABI is a release contract: any change to an exported function's signature or struct layout is a breaking change for everyone linking against it, even though the Rust source still compiles. So the ABI must be versioned like a public API, and the release must include a harness that links the library and calls a symbol, because "it compiled" does not prove the ABI the host expects is the ABI you shipped.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should feature combinations be tested in CI rather than described only in docs?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because a feature combination that is only described in docs rots silently — a minimal build that no CI lane compiles will break the moment some code path assumes a default-on feature, and nobody discovers it until release day. Building at least the minimal, default, and an expanded combination in CI proves the smallest honest artifact is actually buildable and testable, and catches feature-gating mistakes (missing cfg attributes, accidental cross-feature dependencies) at every commit rather than under deadline pressure. Docs describe intent; CI lanes enforce it.

reviewAnswers.question: What should be smoke tested: the crate graph, the built binary, the image, or all of the above?
reviewAnswers.answer: All of the above, because each catches a different failure class. Crate-graph checks (cargo audit, cargo deny) catch vulnerable or policy-violating dependencies before anything is built; testing the built binary catches functional regressions in the final executable; and testing the image catches runtime-environment failures — missing CA certs, missing loader, wrong user — that a binary running on the build host will never reveal. The chapter's central warning is that the most expensive bug is a green release whose final artifact was never run in its real runtime shape, so the image (and the wasm package and native-library harness) must be smoke tested in addition to the binary, not instead of it.
